Handling Editor: L. McCunn A body of environmental psychology research has demonstrated that the inclusion of natural elements within the
built environment, known as biophilic design, can result in improvements in cognition and affect. The current

duced an additional condition that contained a window with shutters, which allowed for daylight infiltration,
while blocking the view of nature. Paired samples t-test analysis revealed that the nature-view condition had a
significant positive effect on creative fluency (i.e. quantity of output) but not on the quality of creative responses.
Moreover, a Multivariate Analysis of Variance indicated that nature-views significantly enhanced positive affect
and reduced negative affect. In contrast, no significant effect of the environment was observed for tonic and
phasic alertness, and executive attention (i.e. working memory). These results indicate that affect, and specific
cognitive processes, are restored by incorporating biophilic elements into architectural design.

2. Material and methods
2.1. Experiment 1
2.1.1. Participants
A priori G* Power analysis for a two-dependent-means test was
conducted using a moderate effect size of 0.5 and a power level of 0.95
(Faul et al., 2009), indicating a required sample size of 54 participants. A
moderate effect size target was chosen, given the diversity of the task
involved and since it affords sufficient sensitivity to detect effects that
are ’large enough to become aware of in normal experience’ (Cohen,
1988). It is also reasonable to assume that for any organisation or in-
dividual to justify structural changes to the environment (i.e. providing
window views of nature), effects on cognition and emotion would need
to be sufficiently perceivable to justify the associated costs. The sample
for experiment 1 consisted of 55 adult participants with normal or
corrected vision and hearing (37 females, 18 males; Mage =24 years, SD
=9), therefore providing adequate power.
2.1.2. Software and hardware
Two DELL Precision 5820 computers with an Intel Xeon 4. GHz CPU,
32 GB RAM and NVIDIA GeForce GTX1080 Graphics Card were used for
the study. Computer 1 used Unreal Engine™ version 4 and SteamVR™
version 1.8.6 to run the VR environments. A VIVE™ VR headset (2160 ×
1200-pixel resolution; HTC Corporation) displayed the environments to
the participant, while two base station tracking devices tracked their
head position. The VR environment was also displayed on the monitor of
Computer 1, so the researcher could monitor the participant’s view
(Fig. 1). Computer 2 used a Logitech Z150 Multimedia PC speaker and
Presentation 20.2 (Neurobehavioral Systems Inc.) to deliver the audi-
tory cognitive tasks. Participants’ responses were registered using a
computer mouse. All cognitive and behavioural tasks were delivered in
an auditory format to avoid interference with the visual environment.
2.1.3. VR environment
Unity was used to create custom-made VR simulating the conditions
(e.g., nature-view and no-window; Fig. 2). In both conditions, the VR
rooms had a floor space of ~20 m2 and had identical office-like features
of white walls, carpet, a wooden desk with a loudspeaker, one door, and
one ceiling lamp. In the nature-view condition, the VR room had three Fig. 2. Simulated Environmental Conditions
